column4: وَالصُّبْحِ إِذَا تَنَفَّسَ makes dawn itself breathe, joining the opening horse's breath to the morning light in a single Quranic image.
God says He made the kindled fire a reminder, confirming the section's reading of brought-forth fire as an admonitory sign rather than a stray detail.
Humans are created from earth, returned into it, and brought out from it once more; burial and emergence are stated as one complete earth-cycle.
God caused humanity to grow from the earth like vegetation, tightening the section's analogy between a field's yield and human bodies.
God returns people into earth and will bring them out with a true bringing-out, directly joining burial to final emergence.
The human asks whether God will gather his bones; جَمْع simultaneously names bodily reassembly and the final gathering developed in the section.
When earth and heavens are changed, all people emerge before the One, the Overwhelming, combining transformed ground, exposure, and universal presence.
وَبَرَزُوا لِلَّهِ جَمِيعًا presents everyone emerging together before God, an exact outer manifestation of the hidden dead into a gathered crowd.
People surge into one another, the trumpet is blown, and God gathers them with a total gathering; moving multitude and assembly converge.
The Godfearing are gathered to the Merciful as a delegation, giving the final crowd a differentiated destination and manner of arrival.
The guilty are driven to Hell وِرْدًا, like a thirsty herd driven to water; the watering-place image becomes a grim final destination.
أَلَا يَظُنُّ أُولَٰئِكَ أَنَّهُمْ مَبْعُوثُونَ confronts exploiters with a rhetorical question about being raised, closely matching the section's unanswered appeal to knowledge.
People stand before the Lord of all worlds on that tremendous day, identifying the destination of the grave-emerging crowd.
After the second trumpet blast, all are standing and looking, a sudden collective emergence into visible awareness.
The earth shines by its Lord, the record is set down, and prophets and witnesses are brought; opened earth, disclosure, and testimony meet.
Every soul comes with a driver and a witness, turning movement to judgment into escorted, adverse testimony.
Each person's deeds are fastened to his neck and God brings out an open record at resurrection, externalizing what had accompanied him unseen.
The record is laid open and people find every deed present; nothing inwardly accumulated is omitted from the final disclosure.
God knows what enters earth and what comes out of it, as well as all descending and ascending, directly framing hidden burial and emergence within divine sight.
God knows what enters the earth and what emerges from it, placing the grave's concealed occupant and final coming-out under one knowledge.
In an actual battle setting God controls the army's perceived size and is declared knowing of what breasts contain, joining outward conflict to inward knowledge.
The resurrection objector is reminded that God created him from a drop before he became an open adversary; his denial itself displays human ingratitude to his Originator.
أَوْسَطُهُمْ, the soundest or most balanced among the garden owners, asks why they did not glorify God; the w-s-ṭ wording places a moral witness in the middle of the dawn party.
God gathers all of them and then questions the associators, joining assembly with the interrogative disclosure of what they had served.
God gathers everyone and questions the angels about the people's worship, another final crowd brought under divine questioning and superior knowledge.
A witness is brought from every community and the Messenger is brought as witness against his people, staging testimony in the assembled judgment.
On the day a witness is raised from every community, deniers receive no leave to answer, making adverse testimony decisive.
God dispersed humanity through earth and to Him they will be gathered, moving from earthly distribution to final collection.
The One who spread humanity through earth is the One to whom they will be gathered, pairing present terrestrial scattering with future assembly.
God gives life, causes death, and then gathers people on resurrection day, stating the whole movement from life through burial to assembly.
The wealthy garden owner's produce is encompassed, and he wrings his hands over what he spent as the garden collapses, a second garden scene where confident possession is overturned.
Qarun comes out in his adornment and people who desire near life wish for his wealth, exposing the attractive force of treasure before earth takes it.
After Qarun is swallowed, his former admirers recognize God's control of provision and the unbeliever's failure, converting desire into belated knowledge.
They feed the needy despite their love of the food, reversing the section's intense attachment by allowing love to remain while giving the loved thing away.
Spending wealth is a grain that grows seven ears and multiplies, turning property and the inner “grain” into productive yield rather than hoarded barrenness.
The command to spend is followed by success for whoever is protected from the soul's stinginess, the direct opposite of the closed hand.
The garden owners finally glorify their Lord and confess wrongdoing, supplying the answer to the central person's rebuke in 68:28.
They acknowledge that they were transgressors, naming the moral nature of the dawn expedition after its reversal.
They hope their Lord will replace the garden with something better, turning failed possession into dependence on the Provider.
God's creative command is simply “Be,” completing the green-tree fire argument with the ease of re-creation.
All dominion belongs to God and all are returned to Him, closing the resurrection answer with its destination.
Garments يُوَارِي nakedness, preserving the covering sense of w-r-y; it illuminates the reversal from covered body to disclosed body, though its immediate subject is clothing rather than burial.
The earth is stretched flat immediately before it casts out and empties what is inside, preparing the exposed ground of 84:4.
The command to fear the Lord is justified by the tremendous quake of the Hour, pairing divine address with earth's final disturbance.
The quake makes people appear intoxicated and breaks ordinary human bonds, supplying the human crowd's condition within the upheaval of 22:1.
At the trumpet God gathers the guilty on that day, a direct formulation of the final assembly initiated by a single sound.
On that day people follow the caller without deviation and voices fall silent before the Merciful, giving the gathered crowd its directed movement and hush.
Every soul is paid fully for what it did, and God knows best their deeds, completing the record-and-witness scene of 39:69.
The veil is removed from the formerly heedless person and sight becomes sharp, making inwardly resisted judgment suddenly perceptible after arrival with witness.
Even when a person presents excuses, the self-insight of 75:14 remains, clarifying why self-witness cannot be evaded.
The assumption that God did not know ruined them, stating the consequence of the mistaken concealment described in 41:22.
The remembered covenant includes “we hear and obey,” followed by the assertion that God knows what breasts contain; pledged witness and inward knowledge meet.
God turns night into day and day into night and knows what breasts contain, extending the section's visible-to-hidden movement under one knowledge.
When asked who sends rain and revives dead earth, people must answer “God”; a question makes land-revival an acknowledged divine act.
Rain brings forth vegetation, clustered grain, and fruit, supplying the productive field and extracted grain against which barren kenūd earth is read.
Water produces varied crops that yellow and become debris, and the sequence is a reminder for people of inner understanding; field change reaches the inward faculty.
The garden owner boasts that he has more wealth and a stronger following, making property the basis of his false security.
He enters his garden while wronging himself and claims it will never perish, the possessive confidence later answered by destruction.
He doubts the Hour and assumes an even better return, linking attachment to his garden with denial of final reckoning.
His companion warns that God may send a calamity from heaven so the garden becomes barren ground, anticipating the owner's reversal.
The warning that its water may sink beyond recovery makes hidden water the boundary of the garden's apparent productivity.
No group can help the garden owner against God after the loss, stripping amassed property of protective power.
Qarun is told to seek the afterlife with what God gave him and to do good, setting use of wealth against possessive accumulation.
Those given knowledge say God's reward is better for faith and good action, opposing informed valuation to the crowd's desire for Qarun's display.
The miserly both command miserliness and conceal what God gave from His bounty, joining withheld property with concealment.
Those who are miserly and command others to be miserly are warned that God is self-sufficient, exposing the hoarder's false stance of independence.
Repulsing the orphan gives concrete social action to the kenūd person's refusal to share what he holds.
Failure to urge feeding the poor directly parallels the garden owners' plan to exclude a needy person.
Withholding ordinary aid distills the closed-hand image into a small, observable refusal.
Failure to urge feeding the poor is named within the causes of punishment, carrying withholding into judgment.
The condemned confess that they did not feed the poor, a final disclosure of the same refusal staged by the garden owners.
The judged person admits that his wealth did not benefit him, reversing the value attached to property before exposure.
His authority has vanished after his wealth fails, completing the stripping away of outward power at judgment.
God gave the denier extended wealth, establishing property as a divine provision toward which his later greed is ungrateful.
He still covets an increase after abundant provision, a concise parallel to acquisitive intensity.
God promises to cast that covetous recipient of wealth into Saqar, taking provision and ingratitude into fire.
God assays the believers and effaces the disbelievers, preserving the refining sense behind the section's image of separating precious substance from residue.
Iron is blown upon until it becomes fire before molten copper is poured, a concrete Quranic meeting of metal, heating, and transformation.
A doubter is shown bones being raised and clothed with flesh, an explicit bodily demonstration of how the dead are brought out again.
God knows people best when He produced them from earth and while they were hidden embryos, extending divine knowledge through successive forms of concealment.
